analysis.one_liner: Lets doctors bill Medicare patients above federal charge limits and void state balance-billing caps.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote in either chamber; it was referred to two House committees and a subcommittee in March 2009 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current Medicare rules, a doctor who does not formally accept Medicare can still bill a patient, but only up to a capped amount above what Medicare pays (the "limiting charge" — 115% of Medicare's approved fee). Several states go further and cap what doctors can charge beyond insurance payments. This bill would do two things: it would let a non-participating physician charge a Medicare patient any amount, with no cap, as long as the practice posted a notice or put language on patient forms saying it does not take Medicare assignment; and it would strike down every state law that limits what a doctor can charge over an insurer's payment. In short, it removes the guardrails that keep doctors from billing Medicare patients far more than Medicare considers reasonable.
analysis.who_benefits: Physicians who do not participate in Medicare (or who treat Medicare patients outside the assignment system) gain the right to bill patients with no limit at all, and to charge beyond what state laws allow. A physician would only need to post a sign or include a line on intake forms saying they do not accept Medicare payment rates — after that, the patient is on the hook for whatever the doctor charges. Practices in states with strong balance-billing protections, which currently cap charges, could collect substantially more from Medicare patients.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the federal limit (currently 115% of Medicare's approved fee) on what a non-participating physician can charge a Medicare patient, as long as the patient was given notice of non-participation.
Preempts all state laws that limit the charges a physician may impose for services, striking down state balance-billing protections.
The required notice is minimal — it may simply be a posting in a conspicuous place in the office or a line on patient information forms.
Changes take effect immediately upon enactment, applying to all services furnished on or after the enactment date.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries. A patient could be billed any amount above what Medicare pays, with no ceiling, and would have little practical recourse — the only protection required is a posted sign or a form line. Patients in states that cap balance billing would lose that protection nationwide, since the federal preemption overrides state law. The people most exposed are seniors on fixed incomes who see a doctor mid-treatment and may never have noticed a wall posting.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare beneficiaries, especially seniors on fixed incomes

drawbacks.text: A Medicare patient could face unlimited out-of-pocket charges above Medicare's approved rate, with nothing in the bill capping the amount — the same service could cost one patient 15% over the Medicare rate and another several times more, at the doctor's discretion.

The notice requirement is extremely weak: a single posted sign in the office or a line on intake forms would satisfy it, so a patient could receive care and then a large bill without a meaningful warning at the moment of service.
It overrides state balance-billing protections in every state, including states that specifically shield patients from excessive provider charges.

The strongest good-faith case for it — that Medicare's limits discourage doctors from treating Medicare patients, and letting them charge market rates would improve access — was never backed by evidence in the legislative record, and the access benefit would flow only to patients able to pay large bills.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated case — that loosening charge limits gives doctors more freedom and might keep more of them seeing Medicare patients — is speculative, while the cost is concrete: seniors would lose the ceiling that currently protects them from charges far above Medicare's approved rates, and states could no longer shield their residents. The notice mechanism is too weak to function as informed consent, since a wall posting does not reach a patient mid-episode of care. On balance the bill's benefits flow to physicians and its costs flow to patients, with no offsetting protection for the people it exposes.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees the day it was introduced, then passed to a subcommittee, and no bill or vote ever came out before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Price of Georgia introduced the bill on March 9, 2009, with seven Republican cosponsors.
The same day, the House referred it to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, each holding it for provisions in its jurisdiction.
On March 10, 2009, the House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health received the referral.
No markup, committee vote, or floor action followed, and the bill expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries came out ahead: because the bill died, the federal cap on what non-participating doctors can charge seniors and all state balance-billing limits remain in place. Physician practices that might have billed above those limits lost the opportunity.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medicare beneficiaries kept their billing protections

against.role: Referral committee; never scheduled markup or action
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 9, 2009, passed it to its Health Subcommittee the next day, and took no further action on the bill.

against.role: Referral committee; never scheduled markup or action
against.what_they_did: Received a concurrent referral on March 9, 2009, and took no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Republican (1 sponsor plus 7 of the chamber's 178 Republicans), and no Democrat signed on; the bill then stalled in committees controlled by the Democratic majority without any recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would remove the 115% cap on what non-participating doctors can charge Medicare patients and void state caps on charges, letting practices bill patients any amount once a sign or form line provides notice. The gain to physician revenue comes directly out of Medicare patients' out-of-pocket costs.

Seniors and disabled beneficiaries would lose both the federal ceiling on excess charges and their states' balance-billing protections, and would be exposed to unlimited bills from doctors who post a notice.
